doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: Heavy metal bars, whiskey sours and staying sober
summary: Playing bars at 14-16 convinced him not to drink; he describes two whiskey sours at 17 and today's healthier musicians.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Did the heavy metal band help you become comfortable on stage?

Maybe. I will tell you this. I was 14, 15, 16 when I was playing heavy metal, and I played in bars, where there was grown-ups, and grown-up stuff was going on. And I learned that I never wanted to consume alcohol at all. I think I became allergic to it just by watching. I thought I don’t want to act like that. You know it’s fine for people who want to do it, that’s fine, they look like they’re having a great time. But I don’t want to look like that. And I remember the only time I’ve ever had a drink on stage I was playing a place called The Estate. I had to be 17 years old, in Milwaukee, a little club. It was hot, and I was playing, it was probably two in the morning and I was doing the thing with all the guys and a couple of women at that point. The women were starting to play more jazz even then. And someone said, “What are you drinking?” I said, “Ginger ale.” Somebody brought me a ginger ale and I just drank it and it was terrible. They said, “You want another?” I said, “Sure” you know. So I had two whiskey sours in about 45 seconds. I didn’t know what they were. I honestly did not know what they were. And the pupils

dilated and at sixteenths and eighths became triplets and what happened? I didn’t like it. I don’t like the experience of being out of control on stage or off. So yes, the heavy metal experience taught me oh, this is what I don’t want to do the rest of my life.

Yeah. I was glad. If I hadn’t encountered that who knows, maybe I would have followed a different route. I’ve still never smoked marijuana my entire life, what kind of a musician am I? And I don’t drink. Although you will probably observe younger musicians — I’m 51 — people younger than me are, the next generation of musicians are the healthiest bunch of people. You know? I mean in Duke’s day at three in the morning, “Let’s go get a steak and a bottle of champagne and some heroin” or whatever. I’m kidding. But I mean it was some very unhealthy things. And today it’s, “I’ll have the vinaigrette black bean soup and the Caesar and the bottle of water. Healthy. Can you believe this? And that’s good. I guess maybe that means that musicians have more self- respect. I don’t know what it is. And maybe the chances of them doing okay are better than they used to be. I mean if you were a jazz musician of a few generations ago it might have been, “Oh a jazz musician, harrumph.” Now it’s okay. Especially, I mean in Europe. My gosh, if you go over there it’s as normal an occupation as working in a bank or selling insurance. “What do you do?” “I’m a musician.” Oh, okay. Over here, “Musician” hum. There’s still a little bit of a stigma but it’s better than it was.
